E17:p1: Then he mounted his riding camel and set off, with the people walking alongside him, until it knelt by the mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Madinah. Some Muslim men were praying there at the time. It was a date-drying yard.
E21:p1: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stopped at Umm Ma‘bad’s tent … She said, “By Allah, we have no food, no milch animal, and no sheep except a ewe that is not producing milk.” The Messenger of Allah ﷺ called for one of her sheep, rubbed its udder with his hand, prayed to Allah, and milked it into a vessel until it foamed. He said, “Drink, Umm Ma‘bad.”
E23:p1: Abu Bakr took all his money with him, five or six thousand dirhams, and set out with it … She took some stones and put them in a niche in the house where my father used to keep his money, then covered them with a cloth.
E24:p1: He took a route going in exactly the opposite direction: the road south of Makkah, leading toward Yemen. He followed this road for about five miles, until he reached a mountain known as Mount Thawr.
E26:p1: They climbed the mountain and passed by the cave. They saw a spider’s web at its entrance and said, “If anyone had gone in here, there would not be a spider’s web at its entrance.” He stayed there for three nights. This is a sound chain of transmission, and it is among the best reports narrated about the spider’s web at the mouth of the cave.
E33:p1: I heard Ibn ‘Ā’ishah say: “When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived in Madinah, the women and children began to say: ‘The full moon has risen over us from the passes of al-Wadā‘.’”
E34:p1: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ left his house on the night of the 27th of Safar, in the 14th year of prophethood, corresponding to September 12/13, 622 CE.
E35:p1: They remained in the cave for three nights: Friday night, Saturday night, and Sunday night.
E36:p1: When Monday night came—the first of Rabi‘ al-Awwal in the year 1 AH, September 16, 622 CE—‘Abdullah ibn Urayqit came to them with the two riding camels.
E39:p1: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived in Madinah, among Banu al-Najjar, on a Friday (12 Rabi‘ al-Awwal, year 1 AH, corresponding to September 27, 622 CE).
H-10637-290-RA-UMM-MIGRATION:p1: Abu Ahmad ibn Bishr ibn Muhammad said: ‘Abd al-Malik ibn Wahb told us: I was informed that Umm Ma‘bad emigrated, accepted Islam, and joined the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Abu Umayyah Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Bishr ibn Muhammad narrated the same.
H-122236-155-CP2-MABAD-ORDER-A:p1: Al-Ṣāliḥī said in *Al-Subul* 3/362–363: In *Al-‘Uyūn*, he mentioned the story of Suraqah before the story of Umm Ma‘bad, and at the outset stated that he was arranging the events chronologically. In *Al-Ishārah*, he mentioned her story before the story of Suraqah, and I followed him in that; this is the correct order, as a number of scholars explicitly stated. I say—
H-122236-156-CP2-MABAD-ORDER-B:p1: Among those who mentioned the story of Suraqah before the story of Umm Ma‘bad are Ibn Ḥibbān in his biography, al-Bayhaqī in his *Dalā’il*, Abu ‘Umar in *Al-Durar*, Ibn al-Jawzī in *Al-Wafā’*, and Ibn Kathīr in *Al-Fuṣūl*, p. 116.
H-12762-1684-CRIT-CAVE1128:p1:
“On the night of the cave, Allah, Mighty and Exalted, commanded a tree, which grew in front of the Prophet ﷺ and concealed him. Allah, Mighty and Exalted, sent a spider, which spun its web between them and concealed the Prophet’s ﷺ face. Allah commanded two wild doves, and they came fluttering (in one copy: flapping) until they settled between the spider and the tree. Young men from Quraysh, one from each clan, came with their sticks, bows, and clubs. When they were about two hundred cubits from the Prophet ﷺ, the guide, Suraqah ibn Malik al-Mudlaji, said, ‘Look at this rock. I don’t know where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ placed his foot.’ The young men said, ‘You haven’t tracked him since last night.’ When morning came, he said, ‘Look in the cave!’ The men went forward, and when they were fifty cubits away, the first one looked and saw the doves, then turned back. They said, ‘What made you turn back instead of looking in the cave?’ He said, ‘I saw two wild doves at the mouth of the cave, so I knew there was no one inside.’ The Prophet ﷺ heard them and realized that Allah, Mighty and Exalted, had used them to ward them off. He prayed for them, and Allah, Exalted is He, protected them in the sanctuary, and they laid the eggs you see.”

Munkar [rejected].

Ibn Sa‘d narrated it (1/228–229), as did al-Mukhallis in al-Fawa’id al-Muntaqah (17/13/1–2), al-Bazzar in his Musnad (2/299/1741, Kashf al-Astar), al-Tabarani in al-Kabir (20/443/1082), al-‘Uqayli (346), and Khaythamah al-Atrabulusi in Fada’il…
H-12762-1687-CRIT-UTHMAN:p1:
“Quraysh consulted one another one night in Makkah. Some of them said, ‘When morning comes, bind him securely,’ meaning the Prophet ﷺ. Others said, ‘Kill him,’ and others said, ‘Rather, drive him out.’ Allah, Mighty and Exalted, informed His Prophet ﷺ of this. That night ‘Ali slept in the Prophet’s ﷺ bed, and the Prophet ﷺ left and reached the cave. The polytheists spent the night keeping watch over ‘Ali, thinking he was the Prophet ﷺ. When morning came, they rushed toward him. When they saw ‘Ali, Allah thwarted their plot. They said, ‘Where is your companion?’ He replied, ‘I don’t know.’ They followed his tracks, but when they reached the mountain they lost the trail. They climbed the mountain and passed by the cave. They saw a spider’s web across its entrance and said, ‘Had he gone in here, there would not be a spider’s web across its entrance.’ He remained there for three nights.”

Ibn Kathir said after it:

“This is a good chain of transmission, and it is among the best reports about the spider’s web at the mouth of the cave.”

That is what he said, but in my assessment it is not good. If ‘Uthman al-Jazari is ‘Uthman ibn ‘Amr ibn Saj al-Jazari, Abu Hatim said of him in al-Jarh wa al-Ta‘dil (3/1/162): “He is not authoritative.” Al-Dhahabi included him in al-Du‘afa’ and said: “He was criticized.” If he is ‘Uthman ibn Saj al-Jazari, without ‘Amr in his name, then the hadith scholar Ibn Hajar leaned in al-Tahdhib toward the view that he is not the former narrator, and his reliability is unknown. He did not distinguish between them in al-Taqrib, where he said: “He is weak.” No one declared Ibn ‘Amr reliable except Ibn Hibban, who is known to be lenient in declaring narrators reliable. Therefore, he is weak and not authoritative, as Abu Hatim said.

Al-Haythami said in Majma‘ al-Zawa’id (7/27): “Ahmad and al-Tabarani narrated it. It includes ‘Uthman ibn ‘Amr al-Jazari, whom Ibn Hibban declared reliable but others considered weak; the rest of its narrators are narrators of the Sahih collections.”

For this reason, the editor Ahmad Shakir said in his commentary on al-Musnad: “There is a problem with its chain of transmission.”
H-12762-1688-CRIT-VERSE:p1:
Furthermore, the previously mentioned verse, “and strengthened him with forces you did not see,” confirms that the hadith is weak, because it clearly states that the victory and support came through forces that could not be seen, whereas the hadith establishes that his ﷺ victory came through a spider, which can be seen. Consider this carefully.

The most likely interpretation of the verse is that the forces were angels, not a spider or two doves. Thus al-Baghawi said in his Tafsir (4/174), commenting on the verse: “They were angels who came down and turned the faces and eyes of the disbelievers away from seeing him.”

Some hadith reports support this meaning. Abu Nu‘aym related from Asma’ bint Abi Bakr: “Abu Bakr saw a man facing the cave and said, ‘Messenger of Allah, he can see us!’ He replied, ‘No. The angels are covering us with their wings now.’ The man soon sat down facing them to urinate. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, ‘Abu Bakr, if he could see you, he would not have done that.’”

Al-Tabarani related it at length in the account of the Hijrah. Al-Haythami said (6/54): “Al-Tabarani related it. It includes Ya‘qub, who is considered good in hadith. The hadith scholar Ibn Hajar said of him: ‘Truthful; he sometimes made mistakes.’”

If there is no other flaw in the chain of transmission, then it is good. However, I cannot state that definitively, because we have often found al-Haythami silent about flaws in hadith, such as a broken chain, tadlis, and the like. That is why he rarely says, “Its chain of transmission is authentic,” or, “Its chain of transmission is good.” Instead, he says, “Its narrators are reliable,” or, “They are deemed reliable,” or, “It includes so-and-so, who is weak,” or, “There is disagreement about him,” and the like. A person familiar with this discipline should therefore not declare a hadith authentic or good based on such phrases from him. If Allah enables us to find the chain of transmission in al-Tabarani or Abu Nu‘aym, we will be able to determine the report’s proper grade. Allah is the One who grants success.

I then found its chain of transmission in al-Tabarani’s al-Mu‘jam al-Kabir (24/106/284), and it became clear that it—
H-12762-921-CRIT-BADR598:p1:
“When he arrived in Madinah, the women, children, and young girls began singing:
‘The full moon has risen over us
From the passes of al-Wada‘.
Gratitude is incumbent upon us
Whenever anyone calls upon Allah.’”
Weak.
Abu al-Hasan al-Khul‘i narrated it in al-Fawa’id (59/2), as did al-Bayhaqi in Dala’il al-Nubuwwah (2/233, edition), from al-Fadl ibn al-Hubab, who said: I heard ‘Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Aishah say—and he mentioned it. This chain is weak. Its narrators are trustworthy, but it is disconnected by the omission of three or more narrators, since this Ibn ‘Aishah was one of Ahmad’s teachers and transmitted it without naming his source.
Al-Hafiz al-‘Iraqi likewise identified this defect in Takhrij al-Ihya’ (2/244). Al-Bayhaqi then said, as quoted in Ibn Kathir’s Tarikh (5/23): “Our scholars mention this when he arrived in Madinah from Makkah, not when he arrived in Madinah via the passes of al-Wada‘ on his return from Tabuk.” Ibn al-Jawzi stated the same view that al-Bayhaqi attributed to the scholars in Talbis Iblis (p. 251, edited by my two colleagues, Professor Khayr al-Din Wanli). But the verifying scholar Ibn al-Qayyim rejected it, saying in al-Zad (3/13): “This is clearly mistaken, because the passes of al-Wada‘ lie in the direction of Syria. Someone coming from Makkah to Madinah would neither see them nor pass by them unless heading toward Syria.”
Despite this, people still see the matter differently from this verification—although, as you have seen, the entire story is unestablished!
(Note): Al-Ghazali included this story with the addition “with tambourines and melodies.” It has no basis, as al-Hafiz al-‘Iraqi pointed out when he said: “There is no mention of tambourines and melodies in it.” Some people were misled by this addition and cited the story with it as evidence that the devotional songs known today are permissible. One may say to them: “First establish the foundation, then build upon it!” Besides, even if the story were authentic, it would not support their position, as was already indicated in the discussion of hadith 579, making repetition unnecessary.
H-12762-9971-CRIT-DRUM6508:p1:
—He arrived in Madinah. When he arrived in Madinah, the Ansar, men and women, came and said, “Come to us, O Messenger of Allah!” He said, “Leave the she-camel, for she has been commanded.” She knelt at Abu Ayyub’s door. He said: Some young women from Banu al-Najjar came out, beating tambourines and singing:

“We are young women from Banu al-Najjar;
How blessed Muhammad is as a neighbor!”

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came out to them and said, “Do you love me?” They replied, “Yes, by Allah, O Messenger of Allah!” He said, “And by Allah, I love you. By Allah, I love you. By Allah, I love you.”

This report, with all these details, is munkar. Al-Bayhaqi included it in Dala’il al-Nubuwwah (2/508), through Abu ‘Abdullah al-Hakim, with his chain of transmission from Muhammad ibn Sulayman ibn Isma‘il ibn Abi al-Ward, who said: Ibrahim ibn Sirma narrated to us; Yahya ibn Sa‘id narrated to us, from Ishaq ibn ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Talhah, from Anas, who said: … Then he related it.
H-12762-9972-CRIT-DRUMCHAIN:p1:
I say: This chain of transmission is weak. Its defect is Ibrahim ibn Sirma—who was al-Ansari. Ibn ‘Adi said in *al-Kamil* (1/252–253): “He narrated from Yahya ibn Sa‘id al-Ansari material that no one else narrates, and no one supports him in any of those reports.” He then said: “Most of his hadiths either have objectionable wording or have their chains confused; the weakness of his reports is clear.” In *al-Lisan* it says: “Ibn Ma‘in said: ‘A wicked liar.’” The narrator from him is Muhammad ibn Sulayman ibn Isma‘il ibn Abi al-Ward, whose biography I could not find. *Al-Jarh wa al-Ta‘dil* (3/269) says: “Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Ansari narrated from … (thus in the original, indicating that it cannot be read). I heard my father say: ‘He is unknown.’” It is possible that this is the same man. Allah knows best.

There is corroboration for the story of the girls and the beating of the tambourine in a hadith from Anas, but it does not say that this happened when he ﷺ arrived in Madinah. Rather, one narration says it happened at a wedding, which is the more likely account—as explained earlier in the analysis of Anas’s hadith, no. 3154, in volume seven of *al-Sahihah*. Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, knows best.

As for what al-Ghazali mentioned in *Ihya’* (2/277) about women singing on rooftops with tambourines and melodies when the Prophet ﷺ arrived:
H-14572-167-CP1-BITE-3:p1:
The flaws in the report:
(1) ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn Ibrahim al-Rasibi.
Imam al-Dhahabi listed him in *Al-Mizan* (2/545), entry (4804), then said:
“‘Abd al-Rahman ibn Ibrahim al-Rasibi, reporting from Malik, brought a long, false report, for which he is the one accused. He also reported from Furat ibn al-Sa’ib, from Maymun ibn Mihran, from Dabbah ibn Muhsin, from Abu Musa, the story of the cave—and it resembles the fabrications of storytellers.”
I say: Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar affirmed Imam al-Dhahabi’s statement about the story of the cave, that it resembles the fabrications of storytellers, in *Lisan al-Mizan* (3/491), entry (602/4953).
(2) Furat ibn al-Sa’ib.
Imam al-Dhahabi listed him in *Al-Mizan* (3/341), entry (6689), then said: “Furat ibn al-Sa’ib, reporting from Maymun ibn Mihran.”
Al-Bukhari said: “His hadith is rejected.”
Ibn Ma‘in said: “He is nothing.”
Al-Daraqutni and others said: “He is abandoned.”
Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: “Regarding Maymun, he is close to Muhammad ibn Ziyad al-Tahhan in that he is accused of the same things as him.” I say: Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar affirmed Imam al-Dhahabi’s statement in *Lisan al-Mizan* (4/503–504), entry (11/6522), then said: “Abu Hatim al-Razi said: ‘His hadith is weak; his hadith is rejected.’ Al-Saji said: ‘They abandoned him.’ Al-Nasa’i said: ‘His hadith is abandoned.’”
I say: Al-Nasa’i’s statement about Furat, “his hadith is abandoned,” is cited in *Al-Du‘afa’ wa al-Matrukin*, entry (488). The statement of Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar in *Sharh al-Nukhbah*, p. 69, is sufficient for you: “It was the position of Al-Nasa’i not to abandon a man’s hadith until everyone agreed to abandon it.”
H-146-244-MABAD-AND-SURAQA:p1: ‘Abd al-Malik said: We were told that Umm Ma‘bad migrated to the Prophet ﷺ and accepted Islam. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ left the cave on Monday night, four nights into the month of Rabi‘ al-Awwal, and arrived at Qudayd on Tuesday. When they departed from there, Suraqah ibn Malik ibn Ju‘shum came upon them on his horse. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed against him, and the horse’s legs sank into the ground. He said, “Muhammad, pray to Allah to free my horse, and I will turn back from you and turn away those behind me.” He did so, and the horse was freed. Suraqah went back and found the people searching for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said, “Go back. I have searched thoroughly for you in this area, and you know how good I am at tracking.” So they turned back.
H-146-249-FRATERNITY-A:p1: Muhammad ibn ‘Umar informed us; Muhammad ibn ‘Abdullah informed us, from al-Zuhri, who said: Musa ibn Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Taymi narrated to us, from his father; ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi al-Zinad narrated to us, from Ibrahim ibn Yahya ibn Zayd ibn Thabit; and Musa ibn Damrah ibn Sa‘id narrated to us, from his father. They said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived in Madinah, he established bonds of brotherhood among the Emigrants, pairing some of them with others, and between the Emigrants and the Helpers. He paired them on the basis of truth and mutual support, and they inherited from one another after death, to the exclusion of their blood relatives. They numbered ninety men: forty-five Emigrants and forty-five Helpers. It is also said that they numbered one hundred, fifty from
H-146-250-FRATERNITY-ANAS:p1: ‘Affan ibn Muslim reported to us: Hammad ibn Salamah reported to us, from ‘Asim al-Ahwal, from Anas ibn Malik, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ established bonds of brotherhood between the Emigrants and the Helpers in Anas’s home.
H-146-250-FRATERNITY-B:p1: There were fifty of the Emigrants and fifty of the Helpers. This was before Badr. When the Battle of Badr took place, Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: “Those related by blood are closer to one another in the Book of Allah. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.” (Surah al-Anfal 8:75) This verse abrogated what had preceded it, ending the inheritance bond of brotherhood. Each person returned to their own lineage, and their blood relatives inherited from them.
H-146-250-MOSQUE-A:p1: (* Muhammad ibn ‘Umar informed us; he said: Ma‘mar ibn Rashid narrated to me from al-Zuhri, who said: The Messenger of Allah’s ﷺ she-camel knelt at the site of the Messenger of Allah’s ﷺ mosque. At that time, some Muslim men were praying there. It was a mirbad belonging to Sahl and Suhayl, two orphan boys from the Ansar who were in the care of Abu Umamah As‘ad ibn Zurarah. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ summoned the two boys and bargained with them for the mirbad, intending to make it a mosque. They said, “Rather, we give it to you as a gift, Messenger of Allah.” But the Messenger of Allah ﷺ refused until he bought it from them. Muhammad ibn ‘Umar said: Someone other than Ma‘mar, from al-Zuhri, said that he bought it from them for ten dinars. He said: Ma‘mar, from al-Zuhri, said that he instructed Abu Bakr to give them that amount. It was an enclosure with walls but no roof, and its direction of prayer faced Jerusalem. As‘ad ibn Zurarah had built it, and he used to pray there with his companions and lead them in the Friday prayer before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered the palm trees in the garden and the gharkad trees there to be cut down. He ordered bricks to be made. There were pre-Islamic graves in the mirbad, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered them to be excavated and the bones removed from sight. There was stagnant water in the mirbad, so they drained it away. They laid the foundations of the mosque and made its length on the side that faced …
H-146-251-MOSQUE-B:p1:
The qiblah side was one hundred cubits from the rear, and the two sides were the same, making it square. It is said that it was less than one hundred cubits. They laid a foundation nearly three cubits high above ground with stones, then built it with mud bricks. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions built it, carrying stones themselves alongside the others and saying:
“O Allah, there is no life but the life of the Hereafter … so forgive the Ansar and the Emigrants.”
He would also say:
“This load is not like the load of Khaybar … This is more righteous, our Lord, and purer.”
He made its qiblah face Jerusalem and gave it three doors: one at the rear, one called the Gate of Mercy, also known as the Gate of ‘Atikah, and a third through which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered, beside the family of ‘Uthman. He made the wall a span in height, its supports palm trunks, and its roof palm fronds. He was asked, “Will you not roof it?” He replied, “A shelter like the shelter of Moses, just a few sticks and grass; there are more pressing matters than that.” He built houses beside it of mud bricks and roofed them with palm trunks and fronds. When the construction was finished, he consummated his marriage to ‘Aishah in the house whose door opened onto the mosque, and placed Sawdah bint Zam‘ah in the other house next to it, by the door beside the family of ‘Uthman.
H-1524-99-CF4-AMAN-WRITERS:p1: Suraqah asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to write him a document. Abu Bakr wrote it for him, though it is said that ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah wrote it for him, on a piece of leather. He then returned, telling people, “You have no need to search here,” and turning the pursuit away from them.
H-1673-1012-HS-PRICE-1:p1:
His words, “Name your price for it” (thāminūnī, with the letter thā’), mean: tell me its price, and I will tell you the price I choose. He said this as part of bargaining, as though he had said, “Bargain with me over the price.”
His words, “We seek no payment for it except from Allah,” mean: we seek no payment, but the matter concerning it rests with Allah. Alternatively, “to” here means “from.” In al-Isma‘ili’s version it is likewise, “We seek no payment for it except from Allah,” and Ibn Majah adds, “ever.” The apparent meaning of the hadith is that they took no payment from him. The historians differ on this, as will be discussed later.
H-1673-4064-NARRATION:p1: Ahmad related, with a good chain of transmission, from Ibn ‘Abbas, concerning the words of the Exalted: “And when those who disbelieved plotted against you”—to the end of the verse. He said: Quraysh consulted one another one night in Makkah. Some of them said, “When morning comes, bind him securely”—meaning the Prophet ﷺ. Others said, “Rather, kill him.” Others said, “Rather, drive him out.” Allah informed His Prophet ﷺ of this, and that night ‘Ali slept in the Prophet’s ﷺ bed, while the Prophet ﷺ left and reached the cave. The polytheists spent the night keeping watch over ‘Ali, thinking he was the Prophet ﷺ—that is, waiting for him to get up so they could do to him what they had agreed upon. When morning came and they saw ‘Ali, Allah thwarted their plot. They said, “Where is your companion?” He replied, “I don’t know.” They followed his tracks, but when they reached the mountain they lost the trail. They climbed the mountain and passed by the cave. They saw a spider’s web across its entrance and said, “Had he gone in here, there would not be a spider’s web across its entrance.” He remained there for three nights.
H-1673-4074-HS-AYYUB-DURATION-1:p1:
His statement, “until it knelt beside the Prophet’s mosque ﷺ in Madinah”: In the report of al-Bara’, from Abu Bakr, the people disputed among themselves as to which of them would host him. He said, “I will stay with my maternal uncles, the descendants of ‘Abd al-Muttalib,” thereby honoring them. In Ibn ‘A’idh’s account, from al-Walid ibn Muslim, and in Sa‘id ibn Mansur’s account, both from ‘Attaf ibn Khalid, it says that the camel first knelt with him. Some people came and said, “The lodging, O Messenger of Allah!” He said, “Leave her.” She set off until she knelt beside the place of the pulpit in the mosque. Then she moved on, and he dismounted. Abu Ayyub came to him and said, “My house is the closest of the houses, so allow me to carry your belongings.” He said, “Yes.” Abu Ayyub carried them and brought the camel to kneel at his house.

Ibn Sa‘d mentioned that when Abu Ayyub carried the Prophet’s ﷺ belongings to his house, the Prophet ﷺ said, “A man is with his belongings.” He also says that Sa‘d ibn Zurara came and took the camel, which then stayed with him. He said, “This is the more firmly established account.” He also mentioned that the Prophet’s stay at Abu Ayyub’s house lasted seven months.
H-1673-4074-HS-MIRBAD-OWNERSHIP-1:p1:
His words, “It was”—that is, the site of the mosque—“a mirbad”: with a kasrah on the mim, a sukun on the ra, and a fatḥah on the ba. It is a place where dates are dried. Al-Asma‘i said: “A mirbad is any place where camels or sheep are penned.” The Basra mirbad was so called because it was where the camel market was held.

His words, “belonging to Suhayl and Sahl”: Ibn ‘Uyaynah added in his *Jami‘*, from Abu Musa, from al-Hasan, that they were both from the Ansar. In al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar’s *Akhbar al-Madinah*, it says that they went to Rafi‘ ibn ‘Amr. Ibn Ishaq says that the Prophet ﷺ asked, “Whose is this?” Mu‘adh ibn ‘Afra’ told him, “It belongs to Suhayl and Sahl, the two sons of ‘Amr, who are orphans in my care, and I will compensate them for it.”

His words, “in the care of Sa‘d ibn Zurarah”: This is how it appears only in Abu Dharr’s version. In the versions of the others it is As‘ad, with an additional alif, which is the correct form. As‘ad was among the first of the Ansar to accept Islam, and he was known by the teknonym Abu Umamah. His brother Sa‘d accepted Islam later. In Ibn Sirin’s mursal report in Abu ‘Ubayd’s *al-Gharib*, it says that they were in the care of Mu‘adh ibn ‘Afra’. Al-Zubayr related that they were in the care of Abu Ayyub. The first account is better established. The reports may be reconciled by saying that they were in the care of more than one person, or that after As‘ad they passed from one person mentioned to another in succession. Ibn Sa‘d mentioned among the virtues of As‘ad ibn Zurarah that he used to pray there before the Prophet ﷺ arrived.

His words, “He bargained with them”: In Ibn ‘Uyaynah’s narration, he spoke to their uncle—that is, the person in whose care they were—to buy it from them. He asked them for it, and they said, “What will you do with it?” He had no choice but to tell them the truth. In Abu Dharr’s version, from al-Kushmihani, it says: “He refused to accept it from them.”

His words, “until he bought it from them”: Ibn Sa‘d related from al-Waqidi, from Ma‘mar, from al-Zuhri, that the Prophet ﷺ instructed Abu Bakr to give them its price. He said: “Someone other than Ma‘mar said that he gave them ten dinars.” In the chapters on mosques, the hadith of Anas has already appeared in which the Prophet ﷺ said, “Banu al-Najjar, name your price for your orchard.” They replied, “No, by Allah, we seek its price only from Allah.” A similar report will come at the end of the following chapter. There is no contradiction between them: they may be reconciled by saying that when they said, “We seek its price only from Allah,” he asked who among them held its title, and they named the two boys, so he bought it from them. In that case, those who said, “We seek its price only from Allah,” may have paid the boys on his behalf. Al-Zubayr says that Abu Ayyub compensated them for its price.
H-1673-4077-HS-FAMILY-1:p1: Ibn Ishaq mentioned that when the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah, he sent Zayd ibn Harithah to bring his wife, Sawdah bint Zam‘ah, his two daughters Fatimah and Umm Kulthum, Umm Ayman—the wife of Zayd ibn Harithah—and her son Usamah. ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr went with them, accompanied by his mother, Umm Ruman, and his two sisters, ‘Aishah and Asma’. They arrived while the Prophet ﷺ was building his mosque. Taken together with her statement, “She gave birth to him at Quba,” this indicates that ‘Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr was born in the first year of the Hijrah, as mentioned earlier.
H-1673-4080-HS-AYYUB-LODGE-1:p1:
His statement, “Which of our family’s houses is closest?” This was explained earlier, at the end of the thirteenth hadith. He called them his family because of the kinship between them through the women: among them was the mother of his grandfather ‘Abd al-Muttalib, Salma bint ‘Awf, of Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar. For this reason, the report of al-Bara’ says that he ﷺ stayed with his maternal uncles—or ancestors—from Banu al-Najjar.

His statement, “Prepare a place for us to rest at midday”: that is, a place where they could take a midday rest. His statement, “Go on,” omits what is understood: he went and prepared it. This is stated explicitly in al-Hakim’s narration, from Abu Sa‘id: “He went and prepared a place for them to rest at midday, then returned.” In the report of Abu Ayyub in al-Hakim and others, it says that he lodged the Prophet ﷺ on the lower floor while he and his family stayed upstairs. He then became concerned about this and continued asking the Prophet ﷺ until the Prophet moved upstairs and Abu Ayyub moved downstairs. Something similar is reported through ‘Abd al-‘Aziz ibn Suhayb, from Anas, by Abu Sa‘id in Sharaf al-Mustafa.

Ibn Sa‘d stated that the Prophet stayed at Abu Ayyub’s house for seven months, until he built his own houses. Abu Ayyub was Khalid ibn Zayd ibn Kulayb, of Banu al-Najjar. Banu al-Najjar were part of al-Khazraj ibn Harithah.
H-1673-4088-HS-QUBA-HOSTS-1:p1:
His words, “Chapter: The Prophet’s ﷺ and his Companions’ arrival in Madinah.” The disagreement about this was explained earlier, at the end of the commentary on ‘Aishah’s long hadith about the Hijrah. He then related through Mu‘tamir ibn Sulayman, from his father, who said: “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abu Bakr arrived wearing white Syrian garments. They passed by ‘Abdullah ibn Ubayy, who stopped to invite him to stay at his home. He looked at him and said, ‘Look for the companions who invited you and stay with them.’ So he stayed with Sa‘d ibn Khaythamah.” Al-Hakim said: “The first report is stronger, and Ibn Shihab knows more about this than anyone else.”

I say: What Abu Sa‘id related in Sharaf al-Mustafa through al-Hakim, via Ibn Mujammi‘, supports Ibn Shihab’s account: “When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed with Kulthum ibn al-Hadm, he and Abu Bakr and ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah were with him. Kulthum said, ‘O Najih’—speaking to a freedman of his—and the Prophet ﷺ replied, ‘You have succeeded.’”

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Zubalah stated in Akhbar al-Madinah that he stayed with Kulthum, who was then a polytheist. What Abu Sa‘id also related, through Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Amr ibn Hazm, supports al-Taymi’s account: “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived at Quba on Monday and stayed with Sa‘d ibn Khaythamah.” He reconciled the two reports by saying that he stayed with Kulthum, but used to sit with his companions at Sa‘d ibn Khaythamah’s home, because Sa‘d was unmarried. If Ibn Zubalah’s account is established, it seems Kulthum’s home was where he spent the night, while he stayed the rest of the time with Sa‘d because Sa‘d had accepted Islam.
H-1673-4089-HS-RECEPTION-GIRLS-1:p1:
His words, “until the slave girls began saying, ‘The Messenger of Allah has arrived’”: In ‘Abdullah ibn Raja’s narration, when he arrived in Madinah, the people came out into the roads and onto the rooftops, along with the boys and servants: “Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, has come! Allah is greatest! Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, has come!” ﷺ. Al-Hakim also related through the chain of Ishaq ibn Abi Talhah, from Anas: “Some girls from Banu al-Najjar came out beating tambourines and saying:

We are girls from Banu al-Najjar …
How welcome Muhammad is as a neighbor!”
H-1673-4094-HS-GRAVES-1:p1:
Regarding his statement, “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered that the graves of the polytheists be dug up, and they were dug up”: Ibn Battal said, “I have found no explicit statement from any of the scholars on digging up the graves of polytheists in order to make the place a mosque. They did, however, differ over whether graves may be dug up to seek treasure: the majority permitted it, while al-Awza‘i prohibited it. This hadith is evidence that it is permissible, because a polytheist has no inviolability, alive or dead. The discussion concerning this matter has already appeared in the chapter on mosques.
Regarding his statement, “And the date palms were cut down”: This is understood to mean that they did not bear fruit. It is also possible that they did bear fruit, but necessity required cutting them down. His statement, “They lined up the date palms,” means the place where the date palms had stood. His statement, “its two doorposts,” with the first letter unvowelled and the second softened, is the dual of ‘idādah: the piece of wood on the side of a door. Every door has two doorposts, and the supports of any object are the parts that brace its sides.
H-1673-4094-HS-MIRBAD-1:p1:
His words, “Name your price for us”: that is, agree on its price with me, or bargain with me over its price. One says, “I bargained with the man over such-and-such,” when one negotiates a price with him.

His words, “for your orchard”: that is, your garden. It was stated in the previous chapter that the place was a mirbad. Perhaps it was originally an orchard enclosed by walls, then fell into ruin and became a mirbad. This is supported by the report that it had palm trees and was in ruins. It was also said that part of it was an orchard and part a mirbad. The owners of the place were named in the previous chapter. Musa ibn ‘Uqbah relates from al-Zuhri that he bought it from them for ten dinars, and al-Waqidi adds that Abu Bakr paid them the money on his behalf.

His words, “There was in it”: he explains this afterward.

His word, “kharib”: with a kasrah on the kha, and fatḥah on the ra and ba. Another explanation was given at the beginning of the Book of Prayer: with a fatḥah on the first letter and a kasrah on the second. Al-Khattabi said: “Most transmitters pronounce it with a fatḥah followed by a kasrah; al-Khayyam related it to us with a kasrah followed by a fatḥah.” He then mentioned possible interpretations, including al-khurub, with a dammah on the first letter and a sukun on the second, meaning circular hollows in the ground; al-jaraf, with a kasrah on the jim followed by a fatḥah on the ra and then an fa, meaning what floodwaters scour away and carry off from the earth; and al-hadab, with an unmarked ha and dal, also meaning raised ground. He said: “This fits the words ‘it was leveled,’ since it is a raised place that is leveled, as is land scoured by floodwaters. Ruins, however, are built up and restored rather than repaired and leveled.” I say: What prevents ruins from being leveled by removing what remains of them and smoothing the ground? One should not give these possibilities weight when the sound narration has an explanation.
H-1681-4456-AMMAR-2812:p1: 2812 — Ibrahim ibn Musa narrated to us: ‘Abd al-Wahhab informed us: Khalid narrated to us, from ‘Ikrimah, that Ibn ‘Abbas said to him and to ‘Ali ibn ‘Abdullah: “Go to Abu Sa‘id and listen to his hadith.” We went to him while he and his brother were in a garden of theirs, watering it. When he saw us, he came over, sat with his legs drawn up, and said: “We used to carry the mosque’s mud bricks one at a time, while ‘Ammar used to carry two at a time. The Prophet ﷺ passed by him, wiped the dust from his head, and said: ‘Alas for ‘Ammar! The rebellious faction will kill him. ‘Ammar calls them to Allah, while they call him to the Fire.’”
H-1681-4718-ASMA:p1: “I prepared provisions for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Abu Bakr’s house when he intended to migrate to Madinah. She said: We could find nothing to tie his provisions or his waterskin with, so I said to Abu Bakr, ‘By Allah, I can find nothing to tie them with except my waist tie.’ He said, ‘Tear it in two and use one piece to tie the waterskin and the other to tie the provisions.’ I did so, and for that reason she was called ‘the woman of the two waist ties.’”
H-1681-5887-HS-AISHA-ARRIVAL-1:p1: “We arrived in Madinah and stayed among Banu al-Harith ibn Khazraj. I fell ill, and my hair came out; then it grew thick and long.”
H-1681-5899-PROVISION:p1: ‘Aishah said: We prepared provisions for the two of them as quickly as we could and packed food for them in a leather bag. Asma’ bint Abu Bakr cut a piece from her waist tie and used it to fasten the mouth of the bag. For this reason, she was called “the woman of the waist tie.”
H-1681-5900-QUBA:p1: Every morning they would go out to the lava plain and wait for him until the midday heat drove them back. One day, after waiting a long time, they returned home. When they had reached their houses, a Jewish man climbed to the top of one of their towers for something he wanted to look at. He caught sight of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions, dressed in white, with the mirage shimmering around them. The Jew could not help calling out at the top of his voice: “Arabs, here is the one you have been waiting for!” The Muslims rushed for their weapons and went to meet the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at the edge of the lava plain. He turned them to the right and led them to Banu ‘Amr ibn ‘Awf. That was on a Monday in the month of Rabi‘ al-Awwal. Abu Bakr stood to address the people, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sat silently. The Ansar who came and had not seen the Messenger of Allah ﷺ began greeting Abu Bakr, until the sun fell upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Abu Bakr came forward and shaded him with his cloak, and then the people recognized the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed among Banu ‘Amr ibn ‘Awf for a little over ten nights. The mosque founded on piety was established, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed in it. Then he mounted his riding camel and set off, with the people walking alongside him, until it knelt by the mosque of the Messenger ﷺ in Madinah. Some Muslim men were praying there at the time. It was a date-drying yard belonging to Suhayl and Sahl, two orphan boys in the care of As‘ad ibn Zurarah. When his riding camel knelt there, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “This, if Allah wills, is the place to stay.” Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ summoned the two boys and negotiated with them for the drying yard so he could make it a mosque. They said: “No, we give it to you, Messenger of Allah.” He then built it as a mosque. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ began carrying mud bricks with them as they built it, saying as he carried the bricks:
H-1681-5905-HS-ANAS-ARRIVAL-1:p1: 3911 — Muhammad related to me: ‘Abd al-Samad related to us: my father related to us: ‘Abd al-‘Azīz ibn Ṣuhayb related to us: Anas ibn Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “The Prophet of Allah ﷺ came to Madinah with Abu Bakr riding behind him. Abu Bakr was an older man who was recognized, while the Prophet of Allah ﷺ was a young man who was not recognized. A man would meet Abu Bakr and ask, ‘Abu Bakr, who is this man in front of you?’ He would reply, ‘This man is guiding me on the way.’ A listener might think he meant the road, but he meant the way of goodness. Abu Bakr turned around and saw a horseman who had caught up with them. He said, ‘Messenger of Allah, a horseman has caught up with us!’ The Prophet of Allah ﷺ turned and said, ‘O Allah, throw him down!’ The horse threw him down, then stood up, snorting. The man said, ‘Prophet of Allah, tell me what you want me to do.’ He said, ‘Stay where you are; do not let anyone catch up with us.’ Thus, at the beginning of the day he was an adversary to the Prophet of Allah ﷺ, and by the end of the day he was an armed guard for him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ alighted beside the lava field, then sent for the Ansar. They came to the Prophet of Allah ﷺ, greeted them both, and said, ‘Ride on, safe and obeyed.’ The Prophet of Allah ﷺ and Abu Bakr mounted, and the Ansar surrounded them with their weapons. It was said in Madinah, ‘The Prophet of Allah has come! The Prophet of Allah ﷺ has come!’ The people looked out and said, ‘The Prophet of Allah has come! The Prophet of Allah has come!’ He continued on until he alighted beside the home of Abu Ayyub. While he was speaking with his family, ‘Abdullah heard of his arrival…”
H-1681-5905-HS-ANAS-ARRIVAL-2:p1: …ibn Salam, who was in a date grove belonging to his family, picking dates for them. He hurried to put down the dates he had picked for them and came with them. He heard the Prophet of Allah ﷺ, then returned to his family. The Prophet of Allah ﷺ asked, “Which of our family’s houses is closest?” Abu Ayyub said, “Mine, O Prophet of Allah. This is my house, and this is my door.” He said, “Go and prepare a place for us to rest at midday.” He said, “Both of you, come in with Allah’s blessing.” When the Prophet of Allah ﷺ arrived, ‘Abdullah ibn Salam came and said, “I testify that you are the Messenger of Allah and that you have brought the truth. The Jews know that I am their leader and the son of their leader, the most learned among them and the son of the most learned among them. So summon them and ask them about me before they learn that I have become Muslim, for if they learn that I have become Muslim, they will say things about me that are not true.” The Prophet of Allah ﷺ sent for them, and they came and entered to see him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them, “O community of Jews, woe to you! Fear Allah. By Allah, besides whom there is no god, you know that I truly am the Messenger of Allah and that I have brought you the truth, so become Muslim.” They said, “We do not know that,” they said to the Prophet ﷺ. He said this three times. Then he asked, “What sort of man is ‘Abdullah ibn Salam among you?” They said, “He is our leader and the son of our leader, the most learned among us and the son of the most learned among us.” He asked, “What do you think, then, if he becomes Muslim?” They said, “Allah forbid! He would never become Muslim.” He asked, “What do you think, then, if he becomes Muslim?” They said, “Allah forbid! He would never become Muslim.” He asked, “What do you think, then, if he becomes Muslim?” They said, “Allah forbid! He would never become Muslim.” He said, “Ibn Salam, come out to them.” He came out and said, “O community of Jews, fear Allah. By Allah, besides whom there is no god, you know that he is the Messenger of Allah and that he has brought the truth.” They said, “You are lying.” Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent them away.
H-1681-5911-HS-ROAD-AND-AISHA-FEVER-1:p1: 3917 - Ahmad ibn ‘Uthman told us: Shurayh ibn Maslamah told us: Ibrahim ibn Yusuf told us, from his father, from Abu Ishaq, who said: I heard al-Bara’ relate: “Abu Bakr bought a saddle from ‘Azib, and I carried it with him. ‘Azib asked him about the journey of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said, ‘They had set watchers on us, so we left at night and traveled swiftly throughout the night and the day, until midday. Then a rock came into view, and we went to it; it had some shade. I spread out a fur I had with me for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Prophet ﷺ lay down on it. I went off to clear the area around him, and then I saw a shepherd approaching with a small flock, heading for the rock for the same reason we were. I asked him, “Whom do you belong to, young man?” He said, “I belong to so-and-so.” I asked him, “Do your sheep have any milk?” He said, “Yes.” I asked him, “Will you milk one?” He said, “Yes.” He took a ewe from his flock. I said to him, “Shake the udder.” He milked some milk, and I had a waterskin of water with a cloth over it, which I had set aside for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. I poured it onto the milk until the bottom of it had cooled. Then I brought it to the Prophet ﷺ and said, “Drink, Messenger of Allah.” The Messenger of Allah ﷺ drank until I was satisfied. Then we set out, with the pursuers on our trail.’ 3918 - Al-Bara’ said: ‘I went with Abu Bakr into his family’s home, and there was his daughter ‘Aishah lying down, afflicted with a fever. I saw—’”
H-1681-753-AMMAR-447:p1:
447 — Musaddad narrated to us, saying: ‘Abd al-‘Aziz ibn Mukhtar narrated to us, saying: Khalid al-Hadhdha’ narrated to us, from ‘Ikrimah, who said: Ibn ‘Abbas said to me and to his son ‘Ali: “Go to Abu Sa‘id and listen to his hadith.” We went and found him in a garden, tending it. He took his cloak, sat with his legs drawn up, then began telling us hadith until he came to the account of the building of the mosque. He said: “We used to carry one mud brick at a time, while ‘Ammar carried two at a time. The Prophet ﷺ saw him, brushed the dust off him, and said: ‘Alas for ‘Ammar! [The rebellious faction will kill him.] He calls them to Paradise, while they call him to the Fire.’” He said: “‘Ammar used to say: I seek refuge in Allah from trials.’”

The words in brackets are an addition found in the transmissions of Ibn al-Sakan and Karima and in the al-Saghani copy, but are not established in the transmissions of Abu Dharr and al-Asili. This is the reading preferred by al-Humaydi, Abu Mas‘ud, Ibn Hajar, and al-Mizzi. Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari (1/542): “In the transmission of Ibn al-Sakan, Karima, and others, and likewise in the al-Saghani copy—which he said he collated against al-Farabrī’s own copy—there is an addition that clarifies the meaning and makes clear that the pronoun refers to those who kill him, namely the people of Syria. Its wording is: ‘Alas for ‘Ammar! The rebellious faction will kill him. He calls them …’” He continued with the hadith. “Know that al-Humaydi did not mention this addition in al-Jam‘, and said that al-Bukhari did not include it at all. Abu Mas‘ud said the same. Al-Humaydi said: ‘Perhaps it did not reach al-Bukhari, or perhaps it did and he deliberately omitted it.’ He said: ‘Al-Isma‘ili and al-Barqani included it in this hadith.’ I say: It seems to me that al-Bukhari deliberately omitted it, for a subtle reason: Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri acknowledged that he had not heard this addition from the Prophet ﷺ, which shows that it is interpolated into this transmission. The transmission that makes this clear does not meet al-Bukhari’s criteria. Al-Bazzar related it through Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from Abu Nadrah, from Abu Sa‘id, who mentioned the hadith about building the mosque and carrying bricks one at a time. In it, Abu Sa‘id said: ‘My companions told me—and I did not hear it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ—that he said: “O son of Sumayyah, the rebellious faction will kill you.”’” Ibn Sumayyah is ‘Ammar, and Sumayyah was his mother. This chain meets Muslim’s criteria, and Abu Sa‘id identified who had told him this. In Muslim and al-Nasa’i, through Abu Salamah, from Abu Nadrah, from Abu Sa‘id, he says: “Someone better than me, Abu Qatadah, told me …” and relates it. Al-Bukhari therefore confined himself to what Abu Sa‘id had heard directly from the Prophet ﷺ, leaving out anything else. This shows the precision of his understanding and his extensive knowledge of the hidden defects in hadith.
Al-Mizzi said in Tuhfat al-Ashraf (3/427): “(Al-Bukhari) Hadith: Ibn ‘Abbas said to me and to his son ‘Ali: ‘Go to Abu Sa‘id and listen to his hadith’ …” The hadith continues to the account of building the mosque, and then to: “‘Alas for ‘Ammar! He calls them to Paradise, while they call him to the Fire.’ He said: ‘“‘Ammar says: I seek refuge in Allah from trials.”’ Al-Bukhari included it in the chapter on prayer (447), from Musaddad, from ‘Abd al-‘Aziz ibn al-Mukhtar; and in the chapter on military expeditions (2812), from Ibrahim ibn Musa, from ‘Abd al-Wahhab al-Thaqafi. Both related it from Khalid al-Hadhdha’, from him, but neither includes: ‘The rebellious faction will kill ‘Ammar.’” Abu Bakr al-Khallal said in al-Muntakhab min al-‘Ilal (131): “Isma‘il al-Saffar informed us: I heard Abu Umayyah Muhammad ibn Ibrahim say: I heard them mention ‘The rebellious faction will kill ‘Ammar’ in the study circle of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Yahya ibn Ma‘in, Abu Khaythamah, and al-Mu‘ayti. They said: ‘There is no sound hadith for it.’” ‘Abdullah ibn Ibrahim said: “I heard my father say: I heard Ahmad ibn Hanbal say: ‘Twenty-eight hadiths have been narrated about ‘Ammar being killed by the rebellious faction, but none of them is sound.’” Ibn Rajab said in Fath al-Bari (3/309): “There was disagreement over the hadith, ‘The rebellious faction will kill ‘Ammar.’ Al-Khallal mentioned in his book al-‘Ilal: Isma‘il al-Saffar told us: I heard Abu Umayyah al-Tarsusi say: I heard them mention ‘The rebellious faction will kill ‘Ammar’ in the study circle of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Yahya ibn Ma‘in, Abu Khaythamah, and al-Mu‘ayti. They said: ‘It is not a sound hadith.’ Al-Khallal said: I heard ‘Abdullah ibn Ibrahim say: I heard my father say: I heard Ahmad ibn Hanbal say: ‘Twenty-eight hadiths have been narrated about ‘Ammar being killed by the rebellious faction, but none of them is sound.’ This chain is not known, and something contrary to this has been narrated from Ahmad. Ya‘qub ibn Shaybah al-Sadusi said in his Musnad, in the section on the Musnad of ‘Ammar: I heard Ahmad ibn Hanbal asked about the Prophet’s ﷺ hadith concerning ‘Ammar, ‘The rebellious faction will kill you.’ Ahmad replied: ‘Just as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: The rebellious faction killed him.’ He said: ‘There is more than one sound hadith from the Prophet ﷺ on this, and he disliked saying more than that about it.’ Al-Hakim said in Tarikh Naysabur: I heard Abu ‘Isa Muhammad ibn ‘Isa al-‘Arid—and he praised him—say: I heard Salih ibn Muhammad al-Hafiz, that is, Jazarah, say: I heard Yahya ibn Ma‘in and ‘Ali ibn al-Madini declare sound the hadith of al-Hasan, from his mother, from Umm Salamah: ‘The rebellious faction will kill ‘Ammar.’”
H-1727-3404-HS-AISHA-FEVER-1:p1: She said: “We arrived in Madinah, and I was ill with fever for a month. My hair grew thick and long.”
H-1727-7453-ROAD-A:p1:
75 - (2009) Salamah ibn Shabib told me: al-Hasan ibn A‘yan told us: Zuhayr told us: Abu Ishaq told us. He said: I heard al-Bara’ ibn ‘Azib say:
Abu Bakr al-Siddiq came to my father’s house and bought a saddle from him. He said to ‘Azib, “Send your son with me to carry it to my home.” My father said to me, “Carry it.” So I carried it, and my father went with him to collect the price. My father said to him, “Abu Bakr, tell me how you spent the night traveling with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.” He replied, “Certainly. We traveled through the whole night until midday, when the road was empty and no one passed along it. Then a tall rock with a patch of shade came into view, untouched by the sun. We stopped there. I went to the rock and smoothed a place with my hands for the Prophet ﷺ to sleep in its shade. Then I spread a fur over it and said, ‘Sleep.’”
H-1727-7453-ROAD-B:p1: “Messenger of Allah, I’ll clear away what is around you.” He slept, and I went out to clear the area around him. Then I saw a shepherd coming with his sheep toward the rock, wanting what we wanted from it. I met him and asked, “Whom do you belong to, young man?” He said, “A man from Madinah.” I asked, “Do your sheep have milk?” He said, “Yes.” I asked, “Will you milk one for me?” He said, “Yes.” He took a ewe. I said, “Shake the udder free of hair, dirt, and debris.” (Al-Bara’ said, “I saw him strike one hand against the other to shake it off.”) He milked some milk for me into a bowl he had with him. I had a waterskin in which I had set aside water for the Prophet ﷺ to drink and perform ablution. I came to the Prophet ﷺ, and I did not want to wake him from his sleep. But when I arrived, he had woken up. I poured water onto the milk until the bottom of it had cooled. I said, “Messenger of Allah, drink some of this milk.” He drank until I was satisfied. Then he said, “Isn’t it time to set out?” I said, “Yes.” We set out after the sun had passed its zenith. Suraqah ibn Malik pursued us. We were crossing a stretch of bare land. I said, “Messenger of Allah, they have caught up with us!” He said, “Do not grieve; Allah is with us.” The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed against him, and his horse sank up to its belly. I think he said, “I know that you two have prayed against me. Pray for me, and I pledge to Allah that I will turn away those pursuing you.” He prayed to Allah, and Suraqah was delivered. He went back, and whenever he met anyone, he said, “I have dealt with what is ahead of you,” and turned them back. He kept his pledge to us.
H-1753-358-CP2-AMAN-WRITERS:p1: (The phrase “Ibn Fuhayrah”): The fā’ has a dammah, the hā’ a fatḥah, and the yā’ is still. It is said that he ﷺ had more than forty scribes. The two who kept his company most closely were Zayd ibn Thābit and Mu‘āwiyah ibn Abī Sufyān after the Conquest; it is also said that it was Abu Bakr. The two reports can be reconciled by saying that Ibn Fuhayrah wrote first and the Truthful One wrote later.
H-23695-189-ARRIVAL-DATES-B:p1: Aside from that, all the scholars refer to this as his arrival in Madinah. In Ibn al-Jawzi’s Sharaf al-Mustafa, Ibn ‘Abbas said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was born on a Monday, received his prophethood on a Monday, lifted the Stone on a Monday, left Makkah as a migrant on a Monday, arrived in Madinah on a Monday, and died on a Monday. In Rawdat al-Aqshahri, Ibn al-Kalbi said: He left the cave on Monday night, on the first day of Rabi‘ al-Awwal, and arrived in Madinah on Friday, twelve nights into the month. Abu ‘Umar said: This is Ibn Ishaq’s account, except for the naming of the day. Abu Sa‘id, in Sharaf al-Mustafa, relates through Abu Bakr ibn Hazm that he arrived on the thirteenth of Rabi‘ al-Awwal. This can be reconciled with the preceding account by attributing the difference to variation in sighting the new moon. In Abu Sa‘id’s account, in a report from ‘Umar, it says: Then he alighted among Banu ‘Amr ibn ‘Awf on Monday, with two nights of Rabi‘ al-Awwal remaining. Perhaps the report should read “two nights had passed,” to match what came before. Ibn Zabalah relates from Ibn Shihab that this was in the middle of Rabi‘ al-Awwal; it is also said that his arrival was on the seventh. Ibn Hazm stated definitively that he left Makkah with three nights of Safar remaining. This agrees with the account of Hisham ibn al-Kalbi, who said that he left the cave on Monday night, the first day of Rabi‘ al-Awwal. If this report is accurately preserved, perhaps his arrival at Quba’ was on Monday, the eighth of Rabi‘ al-Awwal. Combining that with what will be related later from Anas—that he stayed at Quba’ for fourteen nights—would mean that he entered Madinah itself on the twenty-second. But al-Kalbi stated definitively that he entered it when twelve nights of the month had passed. According to his account, he stayed at Quba’ only four nights. Ibn Hibban stated the same definitively: he said that he stayed there on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday—that is, he left on Friday—and did not count the day of departure. Musa ibn ‘Uqbah likewise said that he stayed among them for three nights, apparently counting neither the day of arrival nor the day of departure. Some people of Banu ‘Amr ibn ‘Awf said that he stayed among them for twenty-two days, as Ibn Zabalah relates. In al-Bukhari’s report from Anas, it says, “He stayed among them for fourteen nights.” This is what ‘Aishah meant in her report when she said, “a little over ten nights.” Musa ibn ‘Uqbah related from Ibn Shihab: He stayed among them for three nights. He also said that Ibn Shihab related from Mujammi‘ ibn Harithah that he stayed for twenty-two nights. Ibn Ishaq said that he stayed among them for five days, while Banu ‘Amr ibn ‘Awf claim it was longer. Hafiz Ibn Hajar said: Anas was not from Banu ‘Amr ibn ‘Awf, but from the Khazraj, and he stated definitively that it was fourteen nights, so his account is more worthy of acceptance. The Prophet ﷺ ordered that dates be recorded, and the dating was written beginning with the Hijrah in Rabi‘. Al-Hakim relates this in al-Iklil, but the chain is interrupted. The well-known account is that this happened during ‘Umar’s caliphate, and that ‘Umar said, “The Hijrah separated truth from falsehood, so date by it.” He began the calendar with Muharram, following the suggestion of ‘Ali and ‘Uthman. We have mentioned what has been said about…
H-23833-450-prep-711:p1: Ibn Ishaq said: Al-Husayn ibn ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Amr ibn Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh told me, from Mahmud ibn Labid, who said: When Abu al-Haysar, Anas ibn Rafi‘, arrived in Makkah with a group of young men from Banu ‘Abd al-Ashhal, among them Iyas ibn Mu‘adh, seeking an alliance with Quraysh against their people, the Khazraj, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ heard about them. He went to them and sat with them, then said, “Would you like something better than what you have come for?” They said, “What is that?” He said, “I am the Messenger of Allah. He has sent me to His servants to call them to worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and He has sent down the Book to me.” Then he told them about Islam and recited the Quran to them. Iyas said—
H-23833-451-prep-cont:p1: ibn Mu‘adh, who was a young boy, said, “My people, by Allah, this is better than what you have come for.” Abu al-Haysar, Anas ibn Rafi‘, then took a handful of dust from al-Bathā’ and struck Iyas ibn Mu‘adh in the face with it, saying, “Leave us alone. By my life, we came for something else.” Iyas fell silent. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ got up and left them, and they returned to Madinah. The battle of Bu‘ath between the Aws and the Khazraj took place. He said: Not long afterward, Iyas ibn Mu‘adh died. Mahmud ibn Labid said: Someone from his people who was present when he died told me that they kept hearing him proclaim Allah’s oneness and greatness, praise Him, and glorify Him until he died. They had no doubt that he had died a Muslim; he had embraced Islam at that gathering, when he heard what he heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
H-23833-454-prep-foot-2:p1: Allah Most High mentioned the pledge of the women in the Quran, saying, “They pledge to you that they will not associate anything with Allah” (60:12). By the pledge of the women, he meant that they had not pledged to fight. His pledge with the women was that he took their covenant and promise. When they affirmed it verbally, he said, “I have accepted your pledge.” (See al-Rawd al-Unuf.)
H-23833-472-prep-747:p1: Sa‘d said: “By Allah, I was in their hands when a group of Quraysh appeared before me. Among them was a handsome, fair-skinned, disheveled, good-looking man. I said to myself, ‘If anyone among these people has any good in him, it is this man.’ When he came near me, he raised his hand and struck me hard with his fist. I said to myself, ‘No, by Allah—’”
H-23833-473-prep-cont:p1:
“After this, there is no good in them.” Sa‘d said: “By Allah, I was in their hands as they dragged me when a man who was with them came to my aid. He said, ‘Shame on you! Is there no bond of protection or treaty between you and anyone among Quraysh?’ I said, ‘Yes, by Allah. I used to grant protection to the trade of Jubayr ibn Mut‘im ibn ‘Adi ibn Nawfal ibn ‘Abd Manaf, and I protected them in my land from anyone who wanted to wrong them. I also did this for al-Harith ibn Harb ibn Umayyah ibn ‘Abd Shams ibn ‘Abd Manaf.’ He said, ‘Shame on you! Call out the names of the two men and remind them of what is between you and them.’ I did so, and that man went to them. He found them in the mosque by the Ka‘bah and said, ‘A man from the Khazraj is being beaten in al-Abtah right now. He is calling out to you both and says there is a bond of protection between him and you.’ They asked, ‘Who is he?’ He replied, ‘Sa‘d ibn ‘Ubadah.’ They said, ‘By Allah, he speaks the truth. He used to grant protection to our trade and prevent our people from being wronged in his land.’ They came and freed Sa‘d from their hands, and he went on his way. The man who struck Sa‘d was Suhayl ibn ‘Amr, a man of the Banu ‘Amir ibn Lu’ayy.

Ibn Hisham said: The man who came to his aid was Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham. Ibn Ishaq said: The first poetry composed about the Hijrah was two verses, spoken by Dirar ibn al-Khattab ibn Mirdas, a man of the Banu Muharib ibn Fihr. He said:

‘You rescued Sa‘d by force, then seized him—’”
H-23833-477-AQ-NAMES-CONTEXT:p1:
Ibn Ishaq said: ‘Ubadah ibn al-Walid ibn ‘Ubadah ibn al-Samit told me, from his father al-Walid, from his grandfather ‘Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who was one of the representatives. He said:

“We pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a pledge of war. (‘Ubadah was one of the twelve who pledged allegiance to him at al-‘Aqabah in the First Pledge, the pledge of the women.) We pledged to listen and obey, in hardship and ease, in willingness and reluctance, and even when others were given preference over us; not to dispute authority with those entitled to it; and to speak the truth wherever we were, fearing no blame in the cause of Allah.”
H-23833-490-prep-777:p1:
In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. He said: Abu Muhammad ‘Abd al-Malik ibn Hisham told us; he said: Ziyad ibn ‘Abd Allah al-Bakka’i told us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Muttalibi:

Before the Pledge of al-‘Aqabah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had not been permitted to wage war, nor had bloodshed been made lawful for him. He had only been commanded to call people to Allah, to be patient with harm, and to pardon the ignorant. Quraysh had persecuted those among the emigrants who followed him, until they turned some away from their religion and drove them from their homes. Some had been tempted away from their faith, some were being tortured in their hands, and others had fled through the lands to escape them. Some were in the land of Abyssinia, and some in Madinah, each with their own circumstances.

When Quraysh grew defiant toward Allah and rejected the honor He intended for them, denied His Prophet ﷺ, and tortured and expelled those who worshipped and affirmed His oneness, believed His Prophet, and held fast to His religion, Allah permitted His Messenger ﷺ to fight and to defend himself against those who had wronged and oppressed them. The first verse revealed permitting him to wage war, and making bloodshed and fighting lawful for him against those who oppressed them, as I have heard from ‘Urwah ibn al-Zubayr and other scholars, was Allah’s saying: “Permission to fight is given to those who are fought, because they have been wronged. Allah is surely capable of granting them victory. They are those who were expelled from their homes without right, only for saying, ‘Our Lord is Allah.’ If Allah did not repel some people by means of others, monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques—where Allah’s name is mentioned often—would have been destroyed. Allah will surely help those who help Him. Allah is truly Powerful, Almighty. They are those who, if We establish them in the land, establish prayer and give—”
H-23833-491-prep-778:p1: Ibn Ishaq said: When Allah Most High permitted him ﷺ to fight, and this group of the Ansar pledged allegiance to him to embrace Islam and support him and those who followed him, and Muslims found refuge with them, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ instructed his companions from among the emigrants of his people, and the Muslims with him in Makkah, to leave for Madinah, migrate there, and join their brothers among the Ansar. He said, “Allah has given you brothers and a home where you will be safe.” So they departed in groups, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ remained in Makkah, waiting for his Lord to permit him to leave Makkah and migrate to Madinah.
H-23833-508-807:p1: Ibn Ishaq said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ resolved to set out, he went to Abu Bakr ibn Abi Quhafah. The two of them left through a small door in the back of Abu Bakr’s house, then made for a cave at Thawr—a mountain below Makkah—and entered it. Abu Bakr instructed his son, ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr, to listen during the day for what people were saying about them, then come to them at nightfall with the news of the day. He instructed his freedman, ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah, to graze his sheep during the day, then bring them to rest near the two of them, coming to them in the cave at nightfall. Asma’ bint Abi Bakr would bring them food at nightfall, whatever they needed.
H-23833-509-808:p1: Ibn Ishaq said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed in the cave for three days, with Abu Bakr. When Quraysh lost track of him, they offered a hundred camels to anyone who would bring him back to them. During the day, ‘Abdullah ibn Abu Bakr would stay among Quraysh, listening to what they were planning and what they were saying about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abu Bakr. At dusk, he would go to the two of them and tell them what he had heard. ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah, Abu Bakr’s freedman, would graze with the shepherds of the people of Makkah. At dusk, he would bring Abu Bakr’s sheep to the two of them, and they would milk and slaughter from them. When ‘Abdullah ibn Abu Bakr left them in the morning for Makkah, ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah would follow his tracks with the sheep, covering them up. When the three days had passed and people had ceased searching for them, the man they had hired came to them with their two camels and a camel of his own. Asma’ bint Abu Bakr brought them their provisions, but she had forgotten to bring a cord for tying them. When they set out, she went to hang up the provisions and found there was no cord. So she untied her waist-belt, made it into a cord, and hung them up with it.
H-23833-509-809:p1: For this reason, Asma’ bint Abu Bakr used to be called “the woman with the waist-band.” Ibn Hisham said: I heard more than one scholar say “the woman with the two waist-bands.” The explanation is that when she wanted to tie up the travel provisions, she tore her waist-band in two, tied up the provisions with one piece, and wore the other as a waist-band.
H-23833-509-CONT:p1: Ibn Hisham said: Some people of knowledge told me that al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan al-Basri said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abu Bakr reached the cave at night. Abu Bakr went in before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and felt around inside the cave to see whether there was a wild animal or a snake, protecting the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with his own life.
H-23833-510-811:p1: Ibn Ishaq said: I was told by Asma’ bint Abu Bakr that she said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abu Bakr left, a group of Quraysh came to us, among them Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. They stopped at Abu Bakr’s door, and I went out to them. They said, “Where is your father, daughter of Abu Bakr?” I said, “By Allah, I don’t know where my father is.” She said: Abu Jahl raised his hand—he was vile and wicked—and slapped me so hard that my earring fell off.
H-23833-510-LINEAGE:p1: Ibn Hisham said: Umm Ma‘bad, daughter of Ka‘b, was a woman from Banu Ka‘b of Khuza‘ah.
H-23833-510-PHONE:p1:
She said: Then they departed. We stayed for three nights, not knowing which way the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had gone. Then a man from the jinn came from the lower part of Makkah, singing verses in the style of Arab songs. People followed him, hearing his voice but not seeing him, until he emerged from the upper part of Makkah, saying:

“May the Lord of all people reward with the finest reward
Two companions who stayed at Umm Ma‘bad’s tents.
They stopped there in goodness, then went on at evening;
Fortunate is the one who becomes Muhammad’s companion.
May Banu Ka‘b rejoice in the place of their young woman,
And in her resting place, where the two believers were watched over.”
H-23833-511-814:p1: Ibn Ishaq said: Yahya ibn ‘Abbad ibn ‘Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr told me that his father, ‘Abbad, told him, from his grandmother Asma’ bint Abu Bakr, who said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out, Abu Bakr set out with him. Abu Bakr took all his wealth with him—five or six thousand dirhams—and went off with it. She said: My grandfather Abu Quhafah, who had lost his sight, came in to us and said, “By Allah, I think he has left you bereft by taking his wealth along with himself.” She said: I replied, “No, father! He has left us much good.” She said: I picked up some stones and put them in a niche in the house where my father used to keep his money. Then I covered them with a cloth, took his hand, and said, “Father, put your hand on this money.” She said: He put his hand on it and said, “That is all right. If he has left you this, then he has done well, and it will suffice you.” By Allah, he had left us nothing; I only wanted to reassure the old man that way.
H-23833-511-GUIDE:p1:
Ibn Ishaq said: Asma’ bint Abi Bakr said: “When we heard what he said, we knew where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was headed, and that he was headed for Madinah. There were four of them: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Abu Bakr’s freedman ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah, and their guide, ‘Abdullah ibn Arqat.”
Ibn Hisham said: It is also said that he was ‘Abdullah ibn Uraiqit.
H-23833-514-818:p1:
Ibn Ishaq said: When their guide, ‘Abdullah ibn Urayqit, set out with the two of them, he took them along the lower part of Makkah, then continued with them along the coast until he joined the road below ‘Usfan. Then he took them along the lower part of Amaj, and continued until he joined the road after passing through Qudayd. From there he went on with them along al-Kharrar, then along the mountain pass of al-Marra, then along Liqfa.

Ibn Hisham said: It is also said to be Lafta. Ma‘qil ibn Khuwailid al-Hudhali said:

“A man of noble descent, bringing milk from the people of Laft,
for a clan between Athlah and al-Niham.”

Ibn Ishaq said: Then he took them through the pass of Liqf, then through the narrow valley of Mahaj—called Mijaj, according to Ibn Hisham. Then he traveled with them along the route of Mahaj, then through the route from Dhu al-Ghadwayn—called al-‘Udhwayn, according to Ibn Hisham—then through the valley of Dhu Kashr. Then he took them along al-Jadājid, then al-Ajrad, then along Dhu Salam, from the valley of the enemies of the narrow valley of Ti‘hin, then along al-‘Ababid. Ibn Hisham said: It is also said al-‘Ababib, and al-‘Uthyanah; what is meant is al-‘Ababib.

Ibn Ishaq said: Then he took them through al-Fajj—called al-Qahhah, according to Ibn Hisham.

Ibn Hisham said: Then he brought them down to al-‘Arj. Some of their mounts had fallen behind, so a man from the tribe of Aslam, called Aws ibn Hajr, carried the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to Madinah on a camel of his called Ibn al-Rida’. He sent along with him a young servant of his, called…
H-23833-515-CONT:p1: Mas‘ud ibn Hunaydah. Then their guide left with them from al-‘Arj and took them along the mountain pass of al-‘A’ir, to the right of Rakubah—it is also said to be the pass of al-Gha’ir, according to Ibn Hisham—until he brought them down into the valley of Ri’m. Then he brought them to Quba, to Banu ‘Amr ibn ‘Awf, on Monday, twelve nights into the month of Rabi‘ al-Awwal, when the forenoon had grown hot and the sun was nearly at its zenith.
H-23833-516-822:p1: ‘Ali ibn Abi Talib ﵇ remained in Makkah for three nights and days, until he had returned to people the deposits that they had entrusted to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. When he had finished doing so, he joined the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and stayed with him at the home of Kulthum ibn Hidm.
H-23833-518-827:p1: When it reached the dwellings of Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar, it knelt at the door of his mosque ﷺ. At that time, the place was a drying yard belonging to two orphan boys from Banu al-Najjar, specifically Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar. They were in the care of Mu‘adh ibn ‘Afra’: Sahl and Suhayl, the sons of ‘Amr. When it knelt, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was still mounted. It rose and walked a short distance, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ held its reins without pulling it to turn it. Then it looked behind it, returned to the place where it had first knelt, and knelt there. Then it shifted, snorted, and lowered its neck…
H-23833-519-CONT:p1: …her halter. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ dismounted from her, and Abu Ayyub Khalid ibn Zayd carried his saddle and placed it in his house. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed with him and asked who owned the threshing floor. Mu‘adh ibn ‘Afra’ said to him, “It belongs, O Messenger of Allah, to Sahl and Suhayl, the sons of ‘Amr. They are two orphans under my care, and I will compensate them for it, so make it a mosque.”
H-38114-662-CP1-BRACELETS-A:p1:
*A well-known but weak report:*
As for the well-known report from Suraqah—may Allah be pleased with him—that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: “How...
H-38114-663-CP1-BRACELETS-B:p1:
“Will you wear the bracelets of Kisra?”

During the caliphate of ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab, when the cities were conquered, Kisra’s two bracelets were brought to ‘Umar. He summoned Suraqah ibn Malik, put them on him, and said, “Raise your hands.” Suraqah said, “Allah is the Greatest. Praise be to Allah, who took them from Kisra ibn Hurmuz—the one who used to say, ‘I am the lord of people’—and placed them on Suraqah ibn Malik ibn Ju‘shum, a Bedouin from Banu Mudlij.”

The hadith scholar included this report in *al-Isabah*, and Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr included it in *al-Isti‘ab*, with a broken chain of transmission.

I say: It is established that Kisra’s treasures were brought to ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab. Al-Baghawi related in *Sharh al-Sunnah*, with an authentic chain of transmission, from Ibrahim ibn ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf, who said: When Kisra’s treasures were brought to ‘Umar, ‘Abdullah ibn al-Arqam al-Zuhri said to him, “Will you not put them in the treasury until you distribute them?”

He replied, “No roof shall shelter them until I have distributed them.” He ordered them to be placed in the mosque’s courtyard, and they spent the night guarding them. In the morning, he ordered them uncovered, and he saw among them...
H-7478-1004-RA-BARA-SURAQA:p1: Abu al-Husayn Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Qattan in Baghdad informed us, saying: ‘Abdullah ibn Ja‘far ibn Durustawayh informed us, saying: Ya‘qub ibn Sufyan narrated to us, saying: ‘Ubaydullah ibn Musa and ‘Abdullah ibn Raja’, Abu ‘Umar al-Ghudani, narrated to us, from Isra’il, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara’, who said: “Abu Bakr bought a saddle from ‘Azib for thirteen dirhams. Abu Bakr said to ‘Azib: ‘Tell al-Bara’ to carry it to my saddle.’ ‘Azib said to him: ‘No, not until you tell us what you and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did when you set out and the polytheists were pursuing you.’ He said: ‘We left Makkah at night and traveled through the night and the day until the afternoon. When the midday heat set in, I looked around to see whether there was any shade where we could take shelter. I saw a rock and went to it. There was a patch of shade beside it, so I leveled it. Then I spread a fur for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: “Lie down, Messenger of Allah.” He lay down. Then I went off, looking around me to see whether I could spot any pursuers. Suddenly I saw a shepherd driving his sheep toward the rock, seeking the same thing we were—the shade. I asked him, “Whose shepherd are you, young man?” He said, “A man from Quraysh,” and named him. I recognized the man and asked, “Do any of your sheep have milk?” He said, “Yes.” I asked, “Will you milk one for me?” He said, “Yes.” I told him to catch a sheep from his flock and shake the dust from its udder. Then I told him to shake his hands. He said, “Like this?” and struck one hand against the other. He milked a small amount of milk for me. I had brought a water-skin for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, with a cloth over its opening. I poured water over the milk until the bottom of the container was cool. Then I went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and found that he had woken up. I said, “Will you drink, Messenger of Allah?” The Messenger of Allah ﷺ drank until I was satisfied. Then I said, “It is time to set out, Messenger of Allah.”’
H-7478-1005-RA-BARA-OTHER:p1:
Abu Naṣr ibn Qatādah also informed us, saying: Abu ‘Umar ibn Maṭar informed us, saying: Abu Khalīfah informed us, saying: ‘Abdullah ibn Rajā’ al-Ghudānī narrated it to us, and mentioned it in similar terms.
Al-Bukhārī narrated it in the Ṣaḥīḥ from ‘Abdullah ibn Rajā’, and Muslim included it through another chain from Isrā’īl.
H-7478-1005-RA-BARA-SURAQA:p1: He said: ‘We set out while the people were pursuing us, but none of them caught up with us except Suraqah ibn Malik ibn Ju‘shum, riding his horse. I said, “The pursuers have caught up with us, Messenger of Allah!” He said, “Do not grieve; Allah is with us.” When Suraqah drew near, and there were only two or three spear-lengths between us, I said, “The pursuers have caught up with us, Messenger of Allah!” and I wept. He said, “What makes you weep?” I replied, “By Allah, I am not weeping for myself; I am weeping only for you.” The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed against him, saying, “O Allah, protect us from him in whatever way You will.” Suraqah’s horse sank into the ground up to its belly. He jumped off it and said, “Muhammad, I know this is your doing. Pray to Allah to rescue me from this predicament, and by Allah, I will turn away the pursuers behind me. Here is my quiver; take an arrow from it. You will pass by my camels and sheep at such-and-such a place, so take what you need from them.” The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, “We have no need of your camels or sheep.” The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed for him, and Suraqah went back to his companions. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and I continued until we arrived in Madinah at night.’
H-7478-1008-RA-MUSA-SURAQA:p1:
Abu al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl al-Qattan in Baghdad informed us, saying: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Attab al-‘Abdi informed us, saying: al-Qasim ibn ‘Abdullah ibn al-Mughirah told us, saying:
Isma‘il ibn Abi Uways informed us, saying: Isma‘il ibn Ibrahim ibn ‘Uqbah told me, from his uncle Musa ibn ‘Uqbah, who said: Ibn Shihab told us, saying: ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn Malik ibn Ju‘shum al-Mudliji told me that his father Malik had informed him that his brother Suraqah ibn Ju‘shum had informed him:
“When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ left Makkah as a migrant to Madinah, Quraysh offered one hundred she-camels to anyone who brought him back to them. He said: While I was sitting in the gathering place of my people, a man from among us came and said, ‘By Allah, I have just seen three riders pass by me. I think it was Muhammad.’ He said:
H-7478-1009-RA-MUSA-SURAQA:p1:
“I signaled to him with my eyes to be quiet, and said, ‘They are only so-and-so’s people, looking for a lost animal.’ He said, ‘Perhaps,’ and then fell silent.
He said: I stayed a little while, then got up and went into my house. I ordered my horse to be brought; it was tethered at the bottom of the valley. I took my weapons from behind my living quarters, then took my divining arrows and drew lots with them. I put on my armor, then brought out the arrows and drew lots again. The arrow I disliked came up: ‘He will not be harmed.’ Yet I hoped to bring him back and take the hundred she-camels.
He said: I mounted and followed his tracks. While my horse was carrying me along, it stumbled and I fell off. I brought out my arrows and drew lots again, and the arrow I disliked came up: ‘He will not be harmed.’ But I insisted on pursuing him, so I mounted. When the group came into view and I saw them, my horse stumbled; its forelegs sank into the ground, and I fell off. It pulled its forelegs free, and smoke like dust trailed after them. Then I knew that he had been protected from me and that he would prevail. I called out to them and said, ‘Wait for me! By Allah, I will not harm you, and nothing you dislike will come from me.’
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, ‘Ask him what he wants.’ I said, ‘Write me a document that will be a token between us.’ He said, ‘Write one for him, Abu Bakr.’ He wrote it for me and tossed it to me. I went back and kept quiet; I did not mention anything that had happened. When Allah, mighty and majestic is He, opened Makkah, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had finished with the people of Khaybar, I set out to meet the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, carrying the document he had written for me. As I was making my way to him, I entered among a company of the Ansar. They began prodding me with their spears, saying, ‘Move along, move along,’ until I drew near the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who was on his she-camel. I could see his leg in the stirrup, like a date-palm pith.
